explanations.explanation: David says, “…Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You.” He's standing in a dry land without water, and the thing he's thirsty for is God. Think about that, friend. I bet a lot of us would be dreaming about a cold glass of anything out there, and David's mind goes straight to God.

Good guess, because David does mention a dry and weary land without water. But he doesn't say his soul thirsts for water. He says, “…my soul thirsts for You.” The water is missing, and the One he's longing for is God.
The psalm doesn't mention a road at all. No map, no GPS, no "recalculating." David says, “…Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You.” What he's chasing out there is God.

David says, “So I have seen You in the sanctuary and beheld Your power and glory.” He's remembering a place he's been, and what he took in there was God's power and glory. Out in the dry land, he's still carrying that memory with him. I think a good memory like that is worth packing.

The psalm never mentions priests or an altar. David says he beheld God's "power and glory" in the sanctuary. His eyes weren't on the staff, they were on God. Sounds like he was looking at the right thing.

That's a sanctuary-sounding answer, I'll give you that. But the psalm doesn't say a word about a lampstand. What David says he beheld in the sanctuary is God's "power and glory." Nothing on the furniture list.

David says, “Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You.” The loving devotion comes first, and the glorifying comes right out of it. His lips have a job and they're taking it seriously. Mine mostly say "one more minute" to my alarm clock.
Trust is a fine word, and it's a good thing to do. But in verse 3 David says something else. He says, “…my lips will glorify You.” The word is glorify.
Obey is a good word, friend, but it's not the one David picked here. This verse is about what his lips will do. He says, “…my lips will glorify You.” That's the word that fits the blank.

David doesn't put an end date on it. He says, “So I will bless You as long as I live…” That's not "until I find some water" or "until I'm out of this wilderness." It's as long as he lives, and the psalm doesn't set any other limit.

Right, there's no expiration date on David's blessing. He says, “So I will bless You as long as I live; in Your name I will lift my hands.” Nothing in the verse mentions leaving the wilderness. As long as he lives means as long as he lives. No fine print on that one.

David says, “My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods…” Look at that turn. He began thirsty in a dry land, and now he talks about the richest of foods. The psalm says his joyful lips will praise God. I think a man who sounds that full isn't leaving the table hungry.

I get why you'd pick it, since David did start out thirsty. But verse 5 flips it. He says his soul is satisfied, as with the richest of foods. Starving is where he started looking, and satisfied is where the psalm says he is.

Verse 5 doesn't have David troubled at all. He says, “My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods…” The word is satisfied. And his mouth is busy with praise, so I don't think he's got time to be troubled.

That's what David says: “When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night.” The night is long, and his thoughts stay with God. I think that beats my midnight brain, which delivers a to-do list nobody asked for.

The verse says the opposite. David says, “When I remember You on my bed, I think of You through the watches of the night.” So the bed is where he remembers God, and his thoughts stay there all night. Whatever is on your mind at midnight, friend, David's mind is on God.

explanations.answer: In the shadow of God's wings
explanations.explanation: David says, “For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings.” The help comes first, and the singing comes after it. He doesn't say he'll sing someday when things calm down. He says he will sing for joy in that shadow.

explanations.answer: Within the walls of God's city
explanations.explanation: Walls and a city sound sturdy, but they're not in this psalm. David says, “…I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings.” That's the spot he names. No city limits sign in this one.

explanations.answer: At the top of God's tower
explanations.explanation: No tower anywhere in these verses, friend. Looks like that one was a high climb for nothing. David says, “For You are my help; I will sing for joy in the shadow of Your wings.” He's singing in the shadow, not at the top of anything.

David says, “My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me.” Upholds means holds up. It's like a steady hand under a wobbly tray of cookies that was about to tip. David clings with his soul, and God's right hand upholds him.
Pointing home is a nice picture, but it isn't what David says. He says, “…Your right hand upholds me.” That's about holding him up. The verse doesn't mention a direction at all.
No pushing in this verse, friend. David says, “My soul clings to You; Your right hand upholds me.” God's right hand upholds him, which means it holds him up. David is clinging, and God is holding.

David says, “But those who seek my life to destroy it will go into the depths of the earth.” That's a heavy line, and I think it's okay to let it be heavy. The psalm turns here from David's praise to the ones who seek his life. I'm not going to joke on this one.

The verse says it plainly. David says, “But those who seek my life to destroy it will go into the depths of the earth.” This is a heavy part of the psalm, friend. It comes right after David talks about clinging to God.

The psalm closes with, “But the king will rejoice in God…” After all that thirst and all those heavy words, the last note is rejoicing in God. The psalm doesn't say more about which king, so I won't either. It ends on joy, and I like that for a closing line.
A priest makes sense in a psalm about a sanctuary. But verse 11 doesn't say priest. It says, “But the king will rejoice in God…” The word is king.
Prophet is a reasonable guess, but verse 11 uses a different word. It says, “But the king will rejoice in God…” Nobody in this psalm is called a prophet. The one rejoicing is the king.

explanations.answer: The mouths of liars will be shut
explanations.explanation: David says, “…all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut.” The reason is right there in the verse. Those who swear by God exult because liars will be silenced. It's a quiet ending, and I think quiet fits.

explanations.answer: The dry land will turn green
explanations.explanation: The dry land is where the psalm starts, but it doesn't turn green here. Verse 11 gives a different reason: “…all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut.” So the reason is about liars, not the land. The land stays out of it.

explanations.answer: The enemies will ask for peace
explanations.explanation: That would be a different ending, but it's not the one David writes. The psalm never has the enemies asking for anything. Verse 11 says, “…all who swear by Him will exult, for the mouths of liars will be shut.” The reason is that liars will be silenced.
